source.title: The four numbers that run everything
source.aim: pH, TA, alcohol, free SO₂ — what each one is, why the others matter when you touch one, and what changes them in a tank.
source.application: These are the four numbers Owen watches on every tank. This lesson lets you read them like the vintage log they are.

generated.body_md:
### Why four numbers and not forty

Wine has hundreds of measurable compounds. These four earn their place because they govern everything else: microbial safety, sensory balance, chemical stability, and how every addition you make will behave. Change one and you've already moved at least one other. That's the core idea this lesson is built around.

---

### pH — the master lever

pH measures hydrogen ion activity in solution. In wine, it typically sits between 3.0 and 3.8. That half-unit range sounds narrow; the chemistry it controls is not.

- **Microbial safety.** Spoilage bacteria — *Lactobacillus*, *Pediococcus*, *Acetobacter* — are progressively more inhibited as pH drops. A red at 3.8 is a different microbiological environment than one at 3.4.
- **SO₂ efficacy.** This is the critical link. Free SO₂ exists in three forms in wine; only the molecular form (H₂SO₃) is antimicrobial. The proportion of molecular SO₂ roughly doubles for every 0.3-unit drop in pH. A wine at pH 3.2 needs far less free SO₂ to achieve the same protection as one at pH 3.6.
- **Colour.** In reds, anthocyanins shift toward their more intensely coloured forms at lower pH.
- **What moves it.** Tartaric acid additions lower pH. Malolactic fermentation (MLF) raises it — malic acid (diprotic, stronger) converts to lactic acid (monoprotic, weaker). Cold stabilisation precipitates potassium bitartrate and can raise pH slightly. Dilution from rain or water additions also raises it.

---

### TA — the buffer beneath the surface

Titratable acidity measures the total acid load in wine, expressed as g/L tartaric acid equivalents. Typical wine range: 5–8 g/L. TA and pH are related but not the same thing — two wines can share a pH and have meaningfully different TAs, which affects how they respond to additions and how they taste.

- **Sensory.** TA drives the perception of freshness and structure. Low TA wines feel flat; high TA wines can feel aggressive, especially if pH is also low.
- **Buffering capacity.** A high-TA wine resists pH change when you add acid or base. This matters when you're calculating tartaric additions — the same addition will shift pH less in a high-TA wine than a low-TA one.
- **What moves it.** Tartaric acid additions raise TA and lower pH. MLF lowers TA (malic acid is consumed; lactic acid has lower titratable contribution). Cold stabilisation removes tartrate and lowers TA. Deacidification with calcium carbonate or potassium bicarbonate lowers TA and raises pH.

---

### Alcohol — the solvent that sets the rules

Ethanol in wine typically runs 11–15% v/v (roughly 8.7–11.8 Baumé at harvest, depending on fermentation efficiency). It's not just a number on a label.

- **Extraction and mouthfeel.** Higher alcohol increases extraction of phenolics during maceration and amplifies the perception of body and heat. It also affects tannin polymerisation over time.
- **Microbial inhibition.** Above about 15% v/v, most wine yeasts and many bacteria are significantly inhibited. Below 11%, microbial risk from residual sugar increases.
- **SO₂ binding.** Acetaldehyde — the primary SO₂ binding compound — is produced during fermentation. Higher fermentation temperatures and stressed yeast produce more acetaldehyde, which binds free SO₂ and increases your gross SO₂ requirement.
- **What moves it.** Fermentation converts sugar to alcohol at roughly 0.6% v/v per 1 Baumé. Harvest Baumé is your starting point; fermentation efficiency, temperature, and yeast strain affect the final conversion. Water additions (where legal) lower potential alcohol. Concentration techniques raise it.

---

### Free SO₂ — the number that only makes sense with pH

Free SO₂ is the fraction of total SO₂ not yet bound to wine components. The target free SO₂ for any wine is meaningless without knowing the pH, because molecular SO₂ — the active fraction — is a function of both.

A working rule: target 0.5–0.8 mg/L molecular SO₂ for wines at bottling. At pH 3.2, that requires roughly 13–20 mg/L free SO₂. At pH 3.6, the same molecular target requires roughly 35–55 mg/L free SO₂.

- **Antioxidant action.** SO₂ scavenges hydrogen peroxide and other reactive oxygen species, protecting wine from oxidation.
- **Antimicrobial action.** Molecular SO₂ disrupts microbial cell membranes. This is why free SO₂ management matters most at the end of fermentation and at bottling.
- **What moves it.** Additions of potassium metabisulfite (KMS) or SO₂ gas raise free SO₂. Oxygen exposure, microbial activity, and reaction with carbonyls (especially acetaldehyde) deplete it. Warm storage accelerates depletion. Every pump-over and rack is an opportunity for loss.

---

### The interdependence — why you can't touch one in isolation

These four numbers form a system:

- Add tartaric acid → TA rises, pH falls → molecular SO₂ proportion increases → your existing free SO₂ is now more effective → you may need less at the next addition.
- MLF completes → pH rises, TA falls → molecular SO₂ proportion drops → free SO₂ that was adequate before MLF is now insufficient → add SO₂ immediately post-MLF.
- Alcohol rises through fermentation → acetaldehyde production binds free SO₂ → gross SO₂ demand increases → monitor free SO₂ through active ferment, not just at the end.

Running these numbers in isolation produces decisions that look right on paper and fail in the tank.

---

**What to do this vintage:** Pull the last bench reading for each tank in your cellar brief and check whether the free SO₂ target was set against the current pH or a default figure — they're often not the same wine. If any tank has completed MLF in the last two weeks without a post-MLF SO₂ addition, treat that as urgent.
